editorial:
F.W. Murnau's '4 Devils' (1928) was the director's second Fox production, released in the same year as 'Sunrise' transformed his American career. Shot partly on location with real circus performers and on elaborate Fox studio sets, it followed four orphan acrobats â€” the 'four devils' of the title â€” from childhood through a romance that fractures their troupe. Janet Gaynor and Charles Morton led the cast. The film was profitable on first release, and Fox briefly issued a part-talkie version in 1929, but almost no prints survived: studio fires and deliberate stock destruction wiped out nearly all copies, leaving roughly nine minutes of fragments split between the Library of Congress and Czech archive holdings.

The surviving footage and all associated production stills are free to reproduce and publish â€” the 1928 Fox copyright carried a maximum US term of 95 years, which expired January 1, 2024, and even a valid 1955â€“1956 renewal could not extend protection past that date. What is not free is any musical score layered onto modern archival copies: because the film is silent, any accompaniment was composed and recorded separately and carries its own copyright. A reuser must either strip the score, substitute a public-domain or self-authored one, or license it independently. No commercial restoration has been released, so there is no additional restoration-rights layer on the image fragments themselves.
faq: Are the surviving fragments of '4 Devils' free to use?

Yes â€” the print is public domain. Fox published the film in 1928, and the 95-year maximum US copyright term expired on January 1, 2024, making renewal history irrelevant. You may reproduce, edit, or redistribute the surviving footage. The exception is any musical score on a modern copy: silent-film accompaniments are separately authored and separately protected. Use the footage without the score, or verify the score's rights before publishing.
Does the largely-lost status of the film create any special rights complications?

No. The film being mostly destroyed does not affect copyright status â€” term expiry applies to published works regardless of how many copies survive. The fragments held by the Library of Congress and Czech archives are public-domain material. Practical complications are logistical rather than legal: obtaining access to archival holdings typically requires contacting the archive directly, and any digitization fee an archive charges is an access fee, not a copyright license.
